alalal-e93396-d1e104.summary: Rubric of Article 6: whether the ancients had to believe everything we now believe about the mediator, or whether four things sufficed: nativity, death, resurrection and coming to judgment.

alalal-e93396-d1e124.summary: Introduces the question on Lombard's report that some think it sufficed for the ancients to believe four things: nativity, death, resurrection and coming to judgment.

alalal-e93396-d1e140.summary: First question: the same reason seems to apply to all articles, so the ancients could believe either all or none implicitly.

alalal-e93396-d1e150.summary: Second question: should the simple now believe these four more explicitly than the others?

alalal-e93396-d1e159.summary: Third question: why these four rather than others?

alalal-e93396-d1e166.summary: Reply: since there was disease, salvation required knowledge of the disease and so of the liberator's birth; belief in his coming was required, implicitly without specifying the mode, except for those given special revelation or taught by them. His presence could liberate only through satisfaction for us, so belief in his death was implicitly required; once satisfaction is believed, its effect, the restoration of lost beatitude, requires implicit belief in resurrection, and the punishment of those who despise such salvation requires belief in the coming to judgment. Because these four follow one another in redemption, they had to be believed more fully.
claims: Nativity, death, resurrection and judgment form the logical sequence of redemption and so had to be believed more fully, at least implicitly.

alalal-e93396-d1e218.summary: This answers the first and third questions.

alalal-e93396-d1e225.summary: Reply to the second: now, since these are celebrated and preached more often, anyone who has been a Christian for some time must believe these four explicitly; implicit faith suffices only perhaps for a newly converted adult.
claims: Established Christians must believe the nativity, death, resurrection and judgment explicitly.

alalal-e93396.summary: Article 6 asks whether the ancients had to believe everything we now believe about the mediator, or only his nativity, death, resurrection and coming to judgment. Albert explains that these four form the logical sequence of redemption. Knowing the disease requires belief in a liberator's coming; liberation requires his satisfying death; satisfaction yields restored beatitude through resurrection; and those who despise salvation are punished at the judgment. So these four had to be believed more fully, though implicitly, except by those who received special revelation. Now, because they are constantly celebrated and preached, established Christians must believe them explicitly; implicit faith suffices perhaps only for new adult converts.
claims: Nativity, death, resurrection and judgment form the logical sequence of redemption and had to be believed, at least implicitly, by the ancients.
Established Christians today must believe these four explicitly.
